evidence.note: Caught that logged val metric was bits-per-token, derived correct per-byte conversion and translated the 0.983 target into a val_loss<2.636 nats stopping criterion — establishing an accurate proxy from the start.
Repeatedly evaluated val_loss during the run, computed drop-per-1000-steps, and extrapolated whether the trajectory would cross threshold, while tracking step time and remaining budget.

Detected divergence: loss exploded when LR schedule bugged upward at step 16000; killed the run, diagnosed the get_lr bug, and restarted — course change driven by the val/loss read, not a fixed step count.

Distinguished plateau (~0.001/1000 steps) from overfit (train 2.32 vs val 2.62 gap) and flagged the 0.977 result as too tight under the grader's ±0.05 proxy noise, choosing a dropout v2 run to reduce the gap.
Tracked v2's val_loss against v1 at matching steps (worse at 9k, better at 14k, final 0.966 vs 0.977), a sustained done-vs-remaining read across runs used to select the better checkpoint.

reasoning: The agent maintained an accurate, continuously updated picture of the val_bpb trajectory against the 0.983 target and against remaining compute, clearing the level-8 anchor by distinguishing plateau vs overfit vs under-training and deciding to stop/fix/re-run based on that read (LR-bug kill, dropout v2). It also reaches into level 10 behavior — recognizing diminishing returns, explicitly reasoning about near-threshold margins under proxy noise, and deliberately reallocating effort to a regularized run rather than grinding a saturated config. It falls just short of a full 10 because effort spanned only two productive runs with limited hyperparameter breadth, so I place it at 9.
